extraction.topology: single-pass baseline (P0) versus eight orchestration pipelines (iterative RAG, supervisor-worker fan-out, topic-mining self-loop, STORM multi-perspective, hierarchical width-and-depth, reactive, sub-query graph, beam search) plus two local-7B agents
extraction.benchmark: 90-query deep-research manifest drawn from DRACO, DeepSearchQA, ResearchQA, LitQA2 and custom queries, scored on a nine-dimension 0-1 rubric by a three-judge cross-family panel (GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 4.1, Claude Sonnet 4.5)
extraction.baseline: single-pass P0 on the same GPT-4o model and identical Bing/arXiv/trafilatura tool layer; also a local Qwen2.5-7B twin, an RL-trained DeepResearcher, a best-of-N resampling control, a matched-token-budget clamp, and a pooled oracle-source arm
extraction.key_results: Overall scores span 0.49 (P0) to 0.67 (P1); zero of ten pairs among the five strongest pipelines separate under the tri-judge robustness criterion. The raw baseline-to-cluster gain of +0.145 falls to -0.003 (full-strength length adjustment) to +0.049 (log-words) once report length is controlled, bounding the length-robust share at roughly 0-0.05. The frontier-vs-7B capability gap is 0.23 (P0 vs P9) and 0.38 (P4 vs P9), larger than the entire GPT-4o architecture span, and orchestrating the 7B backbone adds only +0.014 and +0.067 (n.s.). Clamping P1's token budget toward P0's makes its advantage undetectable (p=0.78). Serving identical pooled oracle sources raises citation quality by +0.162 (95% CI [0.06, 0.26]) while factual accuracy is statistically equivalent to zero within +/-0.05; a claim-level entailment decomposition attributes only ~0.09 of the factual shortfall to retrieval. Rubric-guided inference-time verification adds +0.045 on P0 and +0.038 on P4 against budget-matched controls.
extraction.limitations: Authors state: no full human-calibration pilot (judges certify orderings, not absolute substantive levels; Krippendorff alpha 0.42 overall, 0.13 for factual accuracy); each architecture induces its own retrieval pool so the tool interface but not the evidence set is fixed; compute budget is not equalised (17.5x span from single pass to heaviest pipeline), so architecture is bundled with the compute it spends; benchmark contamination is asymmetric across the frontier-vs-7B contrast; two of three judges share the Anthropic family, giving only 1.65 effective votes; the oracle ceiling is demonstrated at one pooled source tier on the six-pattern top cluster; several probes (ReAct, in-house RL agent, 7B orchestration, Bing-vs-Tavily, verification) are single-judge and post hoc; run noise (sigma ~0.05) approaches the equivalence margin.

evidence_notes.summary: This is the most direct test of RQ1 in the batch: it fixes one model (GPT-4o), one search/extraction tool layer, and one retry policy, then varies only orchestration across eleven deep-research architectures scored by a reliability-audited three-judge panel. The headline is that orchestration has bounded, task-conditional returns: the five strongest pipelines are judge-robustly inseparable, and the raw baseline-to-cluster premium of +0.145 shrinks to a 0-0.05 band once report length is controlled and becomes undetectable once token budget is clamped, so a large share of the apparent architecture effect is really compute and verbosity. For RQ2 it is a rare study that both holds the harness constant and quantifies what happens when it is not: the authors argue that published deep-research systems ship whole stacks in which orchestration, base model and retrieval move together, making any reported gain unattributable. It further separates two ceilings beneath the orchestration layer by serving every architecture identical pooled sources, which lifts citation quality but leaves factual accuracy statistically equivalent to zero, and it shows the frontier-vs-7B capability gap dwarfs every architectural effect measured. The paper also demonstrates a judge-side confound, where citation density earns a provenance-independent bonus from the two Claude judges but a null from GPT-5.2.

quotes.text:
Deep-research agents pairing LLMs with web search are usually compared while orchestration, base
model, and retrieval all change at once, so no difference is cleanly attributable to architecture.

Citation quality
is retrieval-bound, and factual accuracy is synthesis-bound. Neither ceiling is the orchestration layer the
field optimises.
The probe certifies one claim: at matched budget P1’s advantage over P0 is no longer detectable.

extraction.topology: n/a (repository-mining study of configuration artifacts, including subagent definitions that run in their own context alongside a central agent loop)
extraction.benchmark: 2,853 GitHub repositories with agentic-tool configuration artifacts, filtered from 37,249 SEART-sampled non-fork engineered OSS projects
extraction.key_results: Eight repository-level configuration mechanisms are documented across Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor CLI, Gemini CLI and Codex CLI: Context Files, Settings, Skills, Subagents, Commands, Hooks, Rules and MCP. Context Files dominate, appearing in 2,586 of 2,853 repositories (90.6%) and used by 61.5-100% of repositories per tool, with CLAUDE.md the most common single artifact (1,640 files, 34.4%), AGENTS.md next (1,508; 31.6%) and copilot-instructions.md third (1,393; 29.2%). Advanced mechanisms are rare: Skills appear in 158 repositories (601 skills, of which 85.5% carry no additional resources and only 5.8% include a scripts directory) and Subagents in 131 repositories (450 subagents, none using Claude Code's persistent-memory feature). 70.6% of repositories configure a single tool and 493 (17.3%) use AGENTS.md with no tool-specific artifact; CLAUDE.md issues 344 outgoing references, 301 of them to AGENTS.md.
extraction.limitations: Authors state: heuristics detect the presence of configuration artifacts, not whether the corresponding tool is actively used (mitigated by an AI-authored-commit scan covering 72.1% of repositories); for Copilot, Cursor and Gemini the detected files apply to both conversational and agentic modes, so agentic usage cannot be isolated; the engineered-project classification used a single GPT-5.2 labeling run with 2,204 'unsure' cases excluded; only open-source GitHub repositories are covered, with no claim of representativeness for proprietary settings; findings are a point-in-time snapshot (February 2026) of fast-moving conventions.

evidence_notes.summary: This paper supplies the definitional and empirical grounding for what a harness is, distinguishing context (the input to a single model call) from the harness (the software layers that assemble that context, expose tool schemas and manage turn-by-turn state), and naming the practice of configuring that harness 'harness engineering'. Its contribution to RQ1 is descriptive rather than causal: it maps eight repository-level configuration mechanisms across five agentic coding tools and measures their adoption, showing that harness configuration in open source is overwhelmingly static context files, with Skills, Subagents, Hooks and MCP adopted by under 20% of repositories per tool. The paper explicitly does not measure the performance effect of these choices, and the authors flag the absence of controlled evidence as an open problem, calling for controlled studies to determine whether richer configuration improves outcomes over Context Files alone. For RQ2, this is a null case that documents the harness surface area a comparison would need to hold constant: eight mechanisms, layered and frequently cross-referencing, with a risk the authors note of redundant or conflicting instructions when multiple context files coexist.

quotes.text:
The
emerging termharness engineeringextends context engineering,
broadening the focus from a model’s context to the full set of mech-
anisms configured around it.

Harness engineer-
ing in open source today is therefore mostly context engineering.

Future work should assess whether deeper configuration leads
to measurable performance gains, extending early evidence on the
impact ofContext Files[ 16].

extraction.topology: default single-agent coding CLI loops (Codex, OpenCode, Pi) compared against published multi-component security harnesses: MAPTA's coordinator/sandbox/validation roles and PentestGPT V2's typed 38-tool interface with task-difficulty assessment, evidence-guided attack-tree search and a memory subsystem
extraction.benchmark: XBOW validation benchmark (104 containerised web-security challenges, binary flag-retrieval scoring), with metrics pass@1, pass@2, reliable solves, cost and tokens per solve
extraction.baseline: default, minimally modified coding CLI agents run on the same backbone model, time budget, target interface and success criterion; published MAPTA and PentestGPT V2 numbers under the closest available model match
extraction.key_results: Under matched GPT-5, Codex solves 70/104 in each of two passes and 81/104 (77.9%) at pass@2, ahead of OpenCode (57, 54; 67 union) and Pi (58, 46; 65 union), with paired McNemar p=0.015 and p=0.023. Both security-specific prompt variants underperform the shipped default (pass@2 68 and 75 versus 81) while costing more and issuing more tool calls. The architecture residual is +9.6 pp for MAPTA (76.9% vs a 67.3% plain GPT-5 pass@1 average) and +5.2 pp for PentestGPT V2 (85.0% vs 79.8% under GPT-5.2), yet the plain-agent two-pass union reaches 77.9% and 88.5%, matching or exceeding both published scores. Holding the Codex scaffold fixed and only changing the model raises pass@1 from 67.3% (GPT-5) to 79.8% (GPT-5.2) to 92.3% (GPT-5.5), the last exceeding PentestGPT V2's 91% Opus 4.5 headline. MAPTA also reports lower cost per challenge ($0.206) than the plain GPT-5 baseline ($0.266).
extraction.limitations: Authors state: MAPTA and PentestGPT V2 are not rerun inside the study's infrastructure, so those rows are descriptive comparisons against published results rather than architectural ablations; the model-scaling arm changes model and cost cap together and was run sequentially rather than randomised; GPT-5.2 dollar figures are repriced post hoc from recorded tokens; only two passes per condition, which is insufficient for precise per-task probability estimates; random flags prevent literal reuse but do not rule out prior knowledge of public challenge structure; roughly 40 targets needed local image or build repairs; all CLI comparisons use GPT-series models, which may favour Codex; XBOW is a CTF-style benchmark, not a full real-world penetration test.

evidence_notes.summary: This is the clearest single statement of the RQ1 attribution problem in the batch and it tests it directly. The authors argue that autonomous-pentest papers ship a new architecture and a new backbone model together, so a higher solve rate cannot be charged to the harness rather than the model, and they propose a plain coding CLI agent under a matched model, budget, target interface and scoring rule as the missing control condition. Their three-phase design isolates one factor at a time: agent scaffold at fixed model, prompt at fixed agent and model, published architecture against the closest model match, and model generation at fixed scaffold. The result is a middle position that is useful for RQ2: specialised harnesses do retain a positive matched-model residual of 5-10 points, but a repeated plain-agent baseline already reaches or exceeds the published architecture scores in union coverage, and a single generation of model improvement inside an unchanged scaffold moves the score by 12-25 points, far more than the harness residual. The reproducibility checklist the paper proposes is directly relevant to RQ2, because it makes a model-matched plain-agent baseline a reporting requirement rather than an optional control.

quotes.text:
Because these systems
often change both architecture and backbone model, it is difficult
to tell how much performance comes from the harness rather
than from the underlying model.

Future
evaluations should report model-matched plain-agent baselines
before attributing benchmark gains to architecture design alone.

Without these controls, a headline score can conflate model
progress, extra budget, prompt changes, and architecture de-
sign.

extraction.topology: orchestrator-subagent workflow specified at the prompt level as agent roles, instructions, inter-agent communication contracts and workflow hops, iteratively rewritten from pairwise self-comparison history
extraction.benchmark: 30 synthetic open-ended machine-learning research tasks across quantitative finance, robotics and pharmacy, each requiring a full code repository with standardised deliverables, scored by pairwise LLM-as-a-judge comparison (gpt-5.5-max and opus-4.7/4.8-xhigh, three seeds)
extraction.baseline: the same base model at higher test-time reasoning effort (xhigh, max, ultracode, the last being a provider-built dynamic multi-subagent harness), plus the un-evolved initial harness H[0] and a stronger base model (opus-4.7) for the train-time-scaling contrast
extraction.key_results: Two RHI iterations let sonnet-4.6-high+H[2] win 20 of 30 pairwise comparisons against sonnet-4.6-max; one iteration suffices for opus-4.7 to beat both xhigh and max, and two iterations let opus-4.8-high+H[2] beat xhigh, max and the built-in ultracode harness. Normalized cost of opus-4.8-high+H[2] is 1.69 versus 2.19 for max (-23%) and 4.15 for ultracode (-60%), with cache read/write down 32% and 64% respectively. Output-token usage stays roughly flat across iterations (1.71-1.86 for sonnet-4.6; 1.42-1.81 for opus-4.8) while win counts rise, decoupling the gain from generation length. Component analysis shows task mutual information rising monotonically for contracts (0.99->1.34 nats) and hops (1.96->2.54) but falling for roles, while task-conditional total correlation among components falls monotonically (4.84->3.63 nats).
extraction.limitations: Authors state: RHI complements rather than replaces train-time scaling, since sonnet-4.6 plus RHI does not consistently close the gap to opus-4.7; the opus-4.7 arm is inconclusive on the token-count confound because output tokens and performance rise together over only two iterations; the embedding-based evidence for the implicit objective is correlational, estimator-dependent and not a proof of the optimizer LLM's true latent objective; only 30 synthetic tasks with pairwise LLM judges and a 30-40% context-budget truncation protocol; the second half of the model-harness co-evolution loop (internalising the traces into future models) is left to future work.

evidence_notes.summary: This paper is the mirror image of the harness-as-confound question: instead of holding the harness fixed it deliberately optimises it while holding the base model fixed, and shows the harness alone can move performance past the plateau of test-time reasoning scaling. That is strong evidence for RQ1, because it demonstrates a large, repeatable performance delta attributable to scaffold and inter-agent contract design with the model, tools and task held constant. Two of its controls are directly useful. First, the authors separate their gains from raw inference scaling by tracking output tokens, cost and cache read/write, and report that token usage stays nearly flat across iterations while win rates rise, so the effect is not simply more generation. Second, they show a prompt-level, task-specific user harness can beat a provider-built system-level multi-agent harness on the same backbone, which implies published comparisons between a bare model and a shipped agent product confound backbone capability with an undocumented orchestration layer. The component analysis localises the improvement to communication contracts and workflow hops rather than agent roles, suggesting the confounding surface is specifically what information flows between agents.

quotes.text:
We show that these gains arise primarily from improved task-specific context
management through more effective inter-agent information flow rather than longer reasoning
traces.

Overall, the gains are notprimarilydriven by longer generations: for two of the three models,
performance improves while output-token usage remains nearly constant.

We interpret this result as
evidence that, on our benchmark, dynamically generating multi-agent workflows through a
provider-built-in harnessis not always sufficient. Instead, atask-specific, user-constructedharness
supplied directly in the prompt can outperform it.

extraction.topology: single-agent ML-engineering scaffolds run per task (AIDE, MLAgentBench, Biomni, STELLA), each with its own internal loop; no cross-agent orchestration
extraction.benchmark: BioML-bench: 24 end-to-end biomedical ML tasks across drug discovery, biomedical imaging, protein engineering and single-cell omics, adapted from the MLE-bench harness and graded by task-specific metrics against expert-populated leaderboards
extraction.baseline: human leaderboard percentiles plus a Dummy agent emitting uninformative (random or zero) predictions
extraction.key_results: Penalized leaderboard percentile: Biomni 34.45+/-5.36, AIDE 28.50+/-5.22, MLAgentBench 21.43+/-4.40, STELLA 20.61+/-5.41, Dummy 2.50+/-1.16; completion rates 100%, 80.2%, 97.9%, 85.4% respectively. Removing the failed-run penalty erases Biomni's consistent lead and makes AIDE competitive (37.41+/-5.85 versus 34.45+/-5.36). All agents average only the 34-37th percentile at best against human leaderboards. Analysis of 41 failed runs attributes them to resource exhaustion, silent try/except errors that skip saving predictions, unnecessary environment creation and uncaught framework exceptions, rather than architectural limits. Deep learning was rarely attempted and almost never selected as the final model even on image tasks, in contrast to human leaderboards dominated by deep learning.
extraction.limitations: Authors state: the choice of LLM backend per agent introduces potential confounds because stronger base LLMs may yield stronger agent performance, and each agent was paired with its own recommended or default model (GPT-4.1 for AIDE and MLAgentBench, Claude Sonnet 4 for Biomni, the OpenRouter default for STELLA), so future work should systematically vary LLMs to disentangle agent design from LLM capability; public leaderboards mix participant expertise, effort and compute budgets; only four agent frameworks and four replicates per agent-task pair were evaluated.

evidence_notes.summary: BioML-bench is a benchmark paper whose main finding is directly on-topic for RQ1: it reports no consistent advantage for biomedical-specialised agents over generalist ML agents and concludes that architecture and scaffolding, not domain specialisation, appear to be the primary drivers of measured capability. It is equally useful as a cautionary case for RQ2, because the study explicitly does not hold the harness or the model constant across arms. Each agent runs its own recommended LLM backend, and the authors name this as a confound in their own limitations section, so the reported percentile differences bundle agent scaffold with backbone capability. The paper also supplies unusually clean evidence that harness quality can dominate a headline metric: the entire ranking flips depending on whether failed runs are scored as zero or excluded, and the authors attribute the failures to addressable scaffolding and execution faults rather than to the agents' architectures. Compute is genuinely matched (identical machine specs, 16-hour GPU and 8-hour CPU wall-clock limits), so the study is partial rather than absent on harness control.

quotes.text:
While performance varies across agents, all agents on average underperform
human baselines; moreover, we observe no consistent advantage for biomedical-specialized over
generalist agents, suggesting that agent architecture and scaffolding may be the primary drivers of
capability at present.

Importantly, these failure modes did not reflect fundamental architectural flaws but
rather are likely addressable issues in scaffolding and execution.

First, the choice of LLMs for agents introduces
potential confounds: stronger base LLMs may yield stronger agent performance.

extraction.framework: LLM4ACOE (LangChain implementation of Sim-HCOME role-playing simulation with three RAG components)
extraction.topology: role-playing simulation of three HCOME roles (Knowledge Engineer, Domain Expert, Knowledge Worker) inside one LLM through iterative discussion, evaluated in a parallel configuration where all RAG components feed one prompt and in a three-step sequential pipeline where one component contributes per step
extraction.benchmark: a human-engineered search-and-rescue (SAR) wildfire reference ontology with 18 competency questions manually converted to SPARQL; precision, recall and F1 on classes, object properties and properties plus percentage of CQs answered
extraction.baseline: the bare-LLM setting with no RAG components enabled (fourth experimental setting), plus the human-generated reference ontology
extraction.key_results: Class F1 by setting: 0.25 (all three RAG components), 0.31 (domain data + ReAct, OWL docs removed), 0.21 (ReAct only), 0.22 (bare LLM), 0.28 (doubled SAR chunk size) and 0.31 (sequential pipeline). CQs answered: 55%, 43%, 50%, 39%, 33% and 59% respectively. The sequential pipeline is best overall, producing 44 classes and 27 object properties with object-property F1 0.22 versus 0.16 for the next best. In the exploratory phase ChatGPT4-o at temperature 0.5 with MMR retrieval answered 14 of 18 CQs (about 78%), against 10.2% for Gemini Pro and 0.9% for Claude Sonnet under the same framework and prompt.
extraction.limitations: Authors state: the LLM is deficient at fully exploiting large amounts of disparate data supplied concurrently, so adding all RAG components at once and doubling domain-data chunk size both degrade coverage; OWL documentation injects domain-irrelevant noise, causing the reuse of a non-existent example ontology and irrelevant classes such as Father, Son and Daughter; responses are inconsistent across iterations and sometimes omit necessary knowledge or add misleading knowledge; the simulated roles are not disjoint because they share the same RAG data, so agents fail to adopt distinct perspectives; human involvement remains crucial for refining and validating the generated ontologies; evaluation covers one domain (SAR) and mainly one LLM.

evidence_notes.summary: This paper is a component-level ablation of a retrieval-and-guidance harness around a fixed LLM, model and prompt, which makes it usable evidence for RQ1 even though its framing is ontology engineering rather than agent evaluation. Across four settings the authors add and remove domain documents, OWL documentation and ReAct thought-action-observation guidelines and observe non-monotonic effects: the fullest configuration is not the best on class F1, doubling the domain-data chunk size makes results worse, and a sequential pipeline that supplies one context source per step outperforms the parallel configuration on every measure. The most transferable finding is that harness context is not additive; supplying more retrieved material concurrently degraded coverage, and the OWL documentation actively injected noise that propagated into the generated artifacts, including the reuse of a fabricated example ontology. For RQ2 the paper is a negative case in one respect that the authors themselves raise: the three simulated agents are not disjoint, sharing the same retrieved context, so the role-playing topology and the retrieval harness cannot be separated from one another in the reported numbers.

quotes.text:
A key ﬁnding of this research is the deﬁciency of the LLM (in this paper, the ChatGPT4-o) to
fully exploit large amounts of disparate data targeting diﬀerent abilities, concurrently.

Conversely the sequential approach adopted in the third experimental phase facilitates the agents to
generate ontologies that are more coherent, and well-structured, while performing better on CQs, achiev-
ing the highest scores.

However, the experimental results also indicate that the roles (agents) are not
disjointed using the same information provided via RAG.

extraction.topology: four framework scaffolds: ReAct-style loop with a curated agent-computer interface (SWE-Agent), general-purpose sandboxed action space (OpenHands), minimal single-bash-tool loop (Mini SWE Agent), and a three-phase fault-localization / context-retrieval / patch-generation pipeline (AutoCodeRover)
extraction.benchmark: SWE-bench Verified Mini (50-task curated subset), 1,200 total runs, 150 runs per framework-model configuration (3 repetitions x 50 issues), with energy measured via Intel RAPL and NVIDIA NVML
extraction.baseline: cross-framework comparison at fixed model, fixed hardware (Intel Xeon w3-2435, RTX A2000 16 GB), 30-minute timeout and 32K context window; no non-agentic or large-model baseline
extraction.key_results: Task resolution is near zero across all configurations: 4% for AutoCodeRover with Qwen-3 1.7B (mean 2 of 50) and 0% for every other framework-model pair. Mean total energy spans 9.4x, from 216.21 kJ (AutoCodeRover/Gemma) and 208.42 kJ (AutoCodeRover/Qwen) down to 23.05 kJ (OpenHands/Gemma) and 23.33 kJ (OpenHands/Qwen). Energy correlates strongly with wall-clock duration (R=0.89) and output tokens (R=0.88) but near zero with memory metrics. Failure signatures differ by architecture: ReAct-style agents are dominated by step repetition leading to context loss, AutoCodeRover by follow-task-requirements and step-repetition failures ending in timeout, and Mini SWE Agent shows low energy that masks premature context-limit terminations and false-positive 'successful' runs that emit destructive or syntactically invalid patches.
extraction.limitations: Authors state: only two small open-weight models and a single hardware configuration were tested, so trade-offs could differ with larger models or other CPU/GPU architectures; SWE-bench Verified Mini's 50 tasks are a small subset of real-world problems; RAPL and NVML capture CPU and GPU only, excluding RAM, storage and wall-plug energy; the binary pass/fail metric ignores partial progress and solution quality; qualitative log analysis was AI-assisted (Gemini 2.5 Flash) with only sampled manual verification; the extremely low resolution rate means conclusions about the energy cost of successful runs are far weaker than those about failed runs.

evidence_notes.summary: SWEnergy holds the model, hardware, timeout, context window and benchmark constant and varies only the agentic framework, which makes it a clean single-factor harness experiment even though its outcome variable is energy rather than accuracy. Its finding is that framework architecture is the primary driver of resource consumption, spanning 9.4x between the most and least energy-intensive scaffolds on the same backbone, while the model's reasoning capacity is the binding constraint on success. That separation of 'the SLM was the bottleneck for success, the framework was the bottleneck for efficiency' is directly relevant to RQ1, because it shows the harness can dominate one reported metric while contributing almost nothing to another under identical conditions. The failure analysis is also useful evidence about retry and recovery policy: high energy is attributed to frameworks allowing the model into unproductive loops with no detection or intervention, and low energy is shown to mask premature termination and false-positive completions with destructive patches. The near-zero resolution rate across the board limits what can be concluded about accuracy, and the authors flag this as a conclusion-validity threat.

quotes.text:
We find that framework architecture is the primary driver
of energy consumption. The most energy-intensive framework,
AutoCodeRover (Gemma), consumed 9.4x more energy on average
than the least energy-intensive, OpenHands (Gemma).

The SLM’s limited rea-
soning was the bottleneck forsuccess, but the framework’s design
was the bottleneck forefficiency.

Second, our experiments were limited to
two small, open-weight models.

extraction.topology: two-agent, turn-based agent-to-agent (AxA) conversation modelled as a partially observable stochastic game, with private internal state, private domain-specific tools and potentially misaligned utilities (customer vs seller; patient vs doctor)
extraction.benchmark: custom AxA benchmark: 66 configurations, 22 customer models x 3 seller configurations, 4 domains (car sales, hotel booking, supply chain procurement, medical consultation), 2,500+ conversations and over 250,000 LLM inferences; echoing detected by a GPT-4o LLM judge validated at 91.1% agreement and Cohen's kappa 0.822 against 150 human annotations
extraction.baseline: the minimal identity-prompt condition, non-reasoning model variants, and conventional task-completion rate as the incumbent metric
extraction.key_results: Echoing rates range from 5% to 70% depending on model and domain. Reasoning models average 32.8% versus 37.7% for non-reasoning, and reasoning effort barely matters (32.7%, 32.8%, 32.9% at low, medium, high). Explicit anti-echoing identity-boundary prompts attenuate but do not eliminate it, with Gemini-2.5-Flash holding 64-73% across all three prompt variants. Echoing onsets on average at turn 7.6 (median 8.0) and echoing conversations run longer (9.6 vs 8.7 turns). 93.2% of conversations complete successfully regardless of identity drift. Requiring a structured response in which the agent explicitly declares its role reduces echoing below 10% across 24 GPT and Sonnet configurations. Open-weight Llama-3.1 models show low rates (11.5% at 8B, 9.1% at 70B), outperforming several larger proprietary models. A cross-model judge ablation gives detection rates of 28.0-46.2% with 79.6-88.9% inter-judge agreement.
extraction.limitations: Authors state: coverage is limited to customer-seller style scenarios in three transactional domains plus one advisory domain, so multi-party, collaborative-planning and long-horizon settings may show different failure modes; the design is asymmetric, varying 22 customer models against only 3 seller configurations; the echoing metric relies on LLM judgment, with GPT-4o the most conservative judge, so reported rates are potentially underestimates; complete elimination of echoing was not the objective; no activation-level analysis of open-weight models was performed.

evidence_notes.summary: Echoing is relevant to RQ1 mainly through its protocol-level mitigation result: holding the model, tools, domain and turn budget fixed and changing only the response schema so that each agent must explicitly declare its role drops the failure rate from 32-38% to below 10%. That is a tool-schema and message-format intervention producing a larger effect than reasoning effort or prompt engineering, which is exactly the kind of harness variable that would confound a topology comparison if left unspecified. The paper also makes a measurement point that bears on RQ2: 93.2% of conversations complete successfully even when identity drift occurs, so conventional task-completion metrics mask the failure entirely, and the authors argue AxA reliability cannot be inferred from single-agent evaluation. The prompt ablation is a useful negative result, since three escalating identity-boundary prompts fail to eliminate echoing in susceptible models, which the authors read as evidence the failure is rooted in post-training alignment rather than in deployment configuration. The experimental design is only partially harness-controlled, since the model sweep is asymmetric and the mitigation arm changes the interaction protocol itself.

quotes.text:
we show that
echoing occurs across major LLM providers, with echoing rates as high as70%
depending on the model and domain.

We further observe that task completion metrics
mask these failures as93%of conversations completed successfully, even when identity drift oc-
curred.

Struc-
tured responses reduced echoing rates to below10%
echoing rates in GPT, Sonnet model variants2.

extraction.framework: Monitor Red Teaming (MRT) workflow with baseline, hierarchical, sequential and mu-hybrid monitor scaffoldings; CUA-SHADE-Arena benchmark
extraction.topology: adversarial agent versus monitoring system; monitor scaffolds are full-trajectory zero-shot prompting, hierarchical summarization over N-tool-call chunks, sequential recursive summarization, and a weighted linear hybrid of the last two, plus a human-in-the-loop escalation layer
extraction.benchmark: SHADE-Arena (17 benign/side task pairs on AgentDojo) and the new CUA-SHADE-Arena (15 pairs built on TheAgentCompany for computer-use agents), with 20 rollouts per agent across 32 tasks; metrics AUC-ROC and TPR at FPR=0.01
extraction.baseline: zero-shot full-trajectory monitor prompting following Kutasov et al., evaluated across unaware/aware/omniscient monitor awareness and unaware/aware agent awareness
extraction.key_results: Against unaware agents every scaffolding reaches AUC >= 0.9. Under agent evasion strategies the baseline scaffolding collapses, in some conditions below AUC 0.5 when monitor hijacking convinces the monitor to output a suspicion score of 1, while the hybrid scaffolding wins AUC at every monitor awareness level (0.75/0.73/0.80 on SHADE-Arena; 0.85/0.84/0.98 on CUA-SHADE-Arena). Across 36 attacker-monitor pairs, monitor AUC correlates with the MMLU-Pro capability gap, but the hybrid shows the weakest association and lets weak monitors such as GPT-4o-mini and Claude 3.6 Haiku exceed 0.85 AUC against all agents. Human-in-the-loop feedback applied to every trajectory lowers both AUC (0.744 to 0.727) and TPR (0.210 to 0.049), whereas a strong prior plus selective escalation of pre-flagged cases raises TPR at 1% FPR from 21.0% to 36.0%.
extraction.limitations: Authors state: only offline monitoring is studied, where the monitor sees a complete trajectory, not the online setting; attacks are elicited by prompting rather than by training a misaligned agent, so fine-tuned attackers remain untested; the sequential, hierarchical and hybrid scaffolds are an initial foray rather than a comprehensive design space; CUA-SHADE-Arena tasks are easier than SHADE-Arena (average unaware trajectory 10,100 versus 25,100 tokens); AUC and TPR are complementary and can move independently; the human overseers were generalists given no specialised grounding tools.

evidence_notes.summary: This is one of the strongest RQ1 results in the batch outside the deep-research setting, because it factorially separates monitor scaffolding from monitor information. Holding the monitor LLM, dataset and threat model fixed, the authors vary only how the agent trajectory is parsed into the monitor (full trajectory, hierarchical summarization, sequential windows, or a hybrid) and separately vary how much the monitor knows about the agent's tasks. The finding is that scaffolding dominates: the hybrid wins AUC at every awareness level and is the most adversarially robust, while giving the monitor more information about the agent yields only trivial advantage once the agent has sophisticated evasion strategies. The paper also demonstrates the practical consequence for RQ2, namely a weak-to-strong scaling effect where a well-designed scaffold lets small monitor models reliably oversee stronger agents, weakening the apparent model-capability scaling law that a baseline scaffolding exhibits. A related confound they surface is that the baseline full-trajectory scaffolding is uniquely vulnerable to prompt injection from the agent, so measured monitor 'capability' partly reflects the parsing harness rather than the model. The human-in-the-loop case study adds that oversight helps only when the escalation policy is targeted.

quotes.text:
First, agent awareness dominates monitor awareness: an agent’s knowledge that it is being monitored
substantially degrades the monitor’s reliability.

Second, monitor scaffolding matters more than monitor awareness:
the hybrid scaffolding consistently outperforms baseline monitor scaffolding, and can enable weaker models
to reliably monitor stronger agents – a weak-to-strong scaling effect .

Therefore,
the most effective way of improving AUC is not by providing the monitor with more information about the agent.
Instead, improving the agent scaffolding from the full trajectory baseline to a hybrid one is more effective.

extraction.topology: single deep-research agent running an interleaved reason-and-search tool loop over a fixed corpus, with an optional whole-document get_document reader tool
extraction.benchmark: BrowseComp-Plus: 830 verified BrowseComp queries over a fixed, human-verified 100,195-document corpus (6.1 evidence documents, 76.28 hard negatives and 2.9 gold documents per query on average); metrics accuracy, evidence recall, search calls, calibration error, plus Recall@k and nDCG@10 for retrievers
extraction.baseline: BM25 as the common lexical retriever paired with every agent; an oracle setting where all labeled positive documents are supplied; the original live-web BrowseComp evaluation as the incumbent protocol
extraction.key_results: Paired with BM25, GPT-5 reaches 55.90% accuracy and Search-R1-32B only 3.86%; swapping BM25 for Qwen3-Embedding-8B lifts GPT-5 to 70.12% while reducing search calls from 23.23 to 21.74. Every agent improves with the stronger retriever, and Sonnet 4 (14.34% to 36.75%) and Opus 4 (15.54% to 36.14%) more than double. Oracle retrieval raises gpt-4.1 to 93.49% versus 14.58% with BM25, and Qwen3-32B to 83.25%, narrowing the open-vs-proprietary gap sharply and localising most of it to interleaved tool use rather than reading comprehension. Adding a whole-document reader tool moves gpt-4.1 from 35.42% to 43.61% but Qwen3-32B only from 10.36% to 11.69%. Raising gpt-oss reasoning effort from low to high improves accuracy (13.37% to 34.58% for 20B with the strong retriever) but multiplies average search calls from about 2 to about 24.
extraction.limitations: Authors state: retrieved documents are truncated to the first 512 tokens for budget reasons, so 13.5% of queries no longer contain the ground-truth answer in a gold document; the corpus was mined with OpenAI o3 plus human verification and only 830 of the original 1,266 queries survive, with 42 Google Maps queries and 13 ambiguous or non-unique answers removed; augmenting with a 10x larger FineWeb corpus mechanically penalises neural retrievers because newly top-ranked documents are unjudged; the role of the retriever during agent optimization or training, and out-of-distribution tool-use generalisation, are left as open questions.

evidence_notes.summary: BrowseComp-Plus is a benchmark built explicitly to remove a harness confound: it argues that live black-box web search APIs conflate agent system performance with retrieval-component effectiveness, making fair comparison and reproducibility impossible, and replaces them with a fixed, human-verified corpus so retrieval and reasoning can be evaluated separately. That is a direct RQ2 case of a study holding one part of the harness constant, and its results quantify how much the un-held part was worth: the same agent with the same prompt and tool interface swings from 55.90% to 70.12% (GPT-5) or from 14.34% to 36.75% (Sonnet 4) purely by changing which retriever backs the search tool, and to 93.49% under oracle retrieval. For RQ1 the implication is that any cross-system deep-research comparison run over different live search backends is measuring the retriever at least as much as the agent. A second harness variable is isolated cleanly too: adding a get_document reader tool to the same agent adds 8.2 points for gpt-4.1 but only 1.3 for Qwen3-32B, showing tool-schema effects interact with model capability rather than adding uniformly.

quotes.text:
Current evaluations of deep-research agents
often conflate agent system performance with the effectiveness of their retrieval compo-
nents, making it difficult to achieve fair and consistent comparisons across systems.
A consistent trend observed across all models is that stronger retrieval leads to higher final accuracy.

In this setup, gpt-4.1 achieves an accuracy of 93.49%. This highlights two key
points. First, it showcases the importance of the retriever: if the retriever is of perfect quality, search
agents can attain substantially high accuracy on complex reasoning tasks in BrowseComp-Plus, in
contrast to the 14.58% baseline accuracy of gpt-4.1 when using BM25 as the retriever.

extraction.topology: n/a (taxonomy over 66 systems: Fine-Tuning, Prompting, Procedural scripted workflows, and Agentic LLM-directed runtime control, with retrieval, program-analysis evidence, test feedback, human feedback and domain knowledge as non-exclusive auxiliary tags)
extraction.benchmark: Defects4J (v1.2/v2.0), SWE-bench (Lite, Verified, Multimodal, full), HumanEval-Java, EvalRepair-Java, QuixBugs, BugsInPy, CVEFixes, PrimeVul and other repair benchmarks as reported by the surveyed systems
extraction.key_results: 66 systems (2022 to April 2026) are coded into Fine-Tuning (21), Prompting (17), Procedural (15) and Agentic (13), with independent-coder agreement of 65/66 on primary paradigm (kappa 0.98) and 64/66 on control subtype (kappa 0.97). Of 2,145 unordered system pairs, only 100 share a recorded benchmark label, 32 fall inside three explicitly bounded comparison windows, 4 additionally share a normalized base-model label, and exactly one pair is model-controlled (MORepair versus Luo et al. on EvalRepair-Java, both within Fine-Tuning), so no model-controlled cross-paradigm comparison exists in the corpus. SWE-bench Lite pass@1 spans 18.00% to 58.30% across eight whole-system stacks. Assurance coding: 10/66 assume perfect fault localization, 7/66 report train/test-style splits, 6/66 narrow scope to single-function or single-hunk repair, 36/66 discuss leakage or contamination, 28/66 report active controls, and 39/66 use validation beyond ordinary public tests. 15 of 29 retrieval-tagged systems target repository-level or industrial settings versus 1 of 37 without retrieval (odds ratio 38.57, Fisher exact p=3.4e-6, BH q=7.2e-5).
extraction.limitations: Authors state: the corpus is criteria-bounded to selected archival venue families plus retained arXiv-only systems rather than an exhaustive census; the survey does not jointly rerun all systems under one benchmark protocol; the retrieval-to-scenario association is descriptive and non-causal because paradigm, scenario, task and publication year are confounded; the benchmark-related prefilter is deliberately permissive and its precision is only spot-audited via a fixed-seed random sample.

evidence_notes.summary: This survey is the most systematic RQ2 evidence in the batch about what happens when the harness is not held constant, because it audits comparability at the level of individual reported results rather than benchmark names. Its central quantitative finding is that across 66 LLM repair systems there are 2,145 possible pairwise comparisons, only 100 share a benchmark label, only 32 fall inside bounded windows, and exactly one pair is model-controlled, and that single pair sits inside one paradigm, so the literature contains no model-controlled cross-paradigm comparison at all. The authors show the same benchmark name can hide different variants, pass@k budgets, fault-localization assumptions, oracle strength and contamination controls, and they deliberately group results into protocol snapshots rather than a leaderboard. For RQ1 the survey's taxonomy is also useful because it separates parameter adaptation from runtime control authority and treats retrieval, analysis, tests and human feedback as orthogonal auxiliary-evidence layers, which is close to the harness/topology distinction, and it reports that within-window score spreads (18.00% to 58.30% on SWE-bench Lite pass@1) must be read as whole-system stacks rather than isolated paradigm effects.

This sole model-

extraction.topology: single-turn and multi-turn (ReAct-style) agent architectures assembled from three tool components: an FHIR Query Generator, a specialized Retriever, and a Code Interpreter
extraction.benchmark: FHIR-AgentBench: 2,931 clinician-sourced questions from EHRSQL-2024 grounded in de-identified MIMIC-IV-FHIR (HL7 FHIR R4) records; metrics are resource-level retrieval precision and recall plus LLM-judged answer correctness
extraction.baseline: a naive full-patient-record in-context prompt (which fails outright, since a full record averages about 3 million tokens as FHIR JSON) and the single-turn agent variants
extraction.key_results: The best configuration, multi-turn with retriever plus code interpreter on o4-mini, reaches only 50.0% answer correctness with precision 0.35 and recall 0.68. Multi-turn interaction raises retrieval recall to about 0.71 versus 0.58 for single-turn. Adding a code interpreter is the largest single lever, lifting correctness from 0.22 to 0.33 in the single-turn setting and from 0.20 to 0.50 in the multi-turn setting at nearly unchanged precision and recall. Across o4-mini, Gemini-2.5-flash, Qwen3 and LLaMA-3.3 the top architecture varies within a narrow 44-50% band. Higher retrieval precision correlates with higher answer correctness even after filtering to questions with perfect recall, showing that flooding context with irrelevant FHIR resources degrades reasoning.
extraction.limitations: Authors state: only single-patient questions are included because multi-patient retrieval latency would dominate evaluation time; unanswerable questions arising from non-existent data sources are not yet covered; all models are restricted to a 32k-token context window; answer correctness is scored by an LLM evaluator (o4-mini) validated at 97% agreement on 500 manually reviewed samples; real-world constraints such as latency and cost are not evaluated.

evidence_notes.summary: FHIR-AgentBench runs a controlled ablation over three harness axes on a fixed benchmark, prompt family and 32k context budget: interaction pattern (single-turn versus multi-turn), retrieval mechanism (direct FHIR API query generation versus a specialized retriever), and reasoning strategy (natural language versus code generation). The result is a clean RQ1 data point that harness composition dominates model choice in this setting: adding a code interpreter to the multi-turn agent more than doubles answer correctness from 0.20 to 0.50 while barely changing retrieval precision or recall, whereas swapping among four models under the same top architecture moves correctness only within a 44-50% band. The authors state this explicitly, concluding that architecture and task difficulty are currently more significant bottlenecks than the base LLM. The paper also isolates a context-management confound relevant to RQ1: the retriever is designed to favour recall over precision, and higher precision correlates with better answers even at perfect recall, so a scaffold that over-retrieves will look worse at reasoning than one that does not, independent of the model.

of the base LLM.

extraction.topology: single RL search agent selecting from a finite, environment-constructed action menu (Select an evidence sentence, Lookup an entity, Answer, Answer_With) over a programmatically induced paragraph-sentence-entity graph, with the environment building queries and updating retrieval state
extraction.benchmark: 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, MuSiQue (multi-hop) and NQ, PopQA, TriviaQA (single-hop), reported as EM, F1, retrieval similarity and generation evaluation; 5,120 training and 128 held-out questions per dataset
extraction.baseline: free-query RL search agents (Search-R1, IGPO, R1-Searcher, Graph-R1), naive generation, standard RAG, SFT, GRPO-only R1, and GPT-4o-mini GraphRAG-family prompt-only systems; plus a transition-matched free-query arm and outcome-only credit arms for ablation
extraction.key_results: Average F1 50.83 at 1.5B (+10.74 over Graph-R1) and 55.24 at 3B (+3.98), with the largest gains on multi-hop datasets (+7.68 average at 3B). Under a transition-matched control that fixes feasible targets, environment transitions, budgets, corpora, reward, seeds and data order, the action menu alone adds more than 17 F1 over free query under both credit regimes and more than 35 on MuSiQue under outcome-only training. Full SNC adds a further 3.08, 4.55 and 2.88 F1 on 2Wiki, HotpotQA and MuSiQue over outcome-only. Free-query rollout groups collapse from roughly 86% spanning multiple retrieval-equivalence classes to below 10% by training step 30, while the menu preserves retrieval-distinct outcomes. SNC requires no extra agent rollouts and adds 9-11% per-step wall-clock; graph construction is LLM-free at $0 API cost and 0.12s per 1K corpus tokens.
extraction.limitations: Authors state: Harness-G is text-only, and extending its structured actions and SNC to multimodal evidence is the key next step; baseline values in the main table are published cross-stack references and only the interface and credit ablation arms are protocol-matched; each held-out split contains only 128 questions, so the authors emphasise large consistent cross-dataset trends over isolated marginal differences; NQ remains a weak point, trailing Graph-R1 by 1.84 F1 at 3B.

evidence_notes.summary: Harness-G is a rare example of an intervention on the tool and action schema itself, with an explicit transition-matched control that answers RQ2 in the affirmative. The authors hold feasible retrieval targets, environment transitions, deduplication, candidate caps, top-K, budgets, corpora, graph indices, initial checkpoints, questions, reward, group size, batch size, training steps, loss masking, data order and seeds constant, so the only difference between arms is whether the policy selects a menu entry directly or reaches the same target through a generated free-form query. Under that control the interface alone accounts for more than 17 F1 points, and more than 35 on MuSiQue under outcome-only training, which is a large effect attributable purely to how actions are exposed to the model rather than to the model, the retrieval substrate or the reward. The diagnostic mechanism is directly relevant to RQ1: the authors document retrieval-equivalence collapse, where free-form queries stay surface-diverse while their accumulated evidence sets converge, so measured 'exploration' in free-query agents is partly illusory. The paper's ablation also separates the interface contribution from the credit-assignment contribution, isolating each factor rather than reporting a bundled system gain.

extraction.topology: multi-agent system with a dual optimization strategy: Planner, Controller and Extractor for global hierarchical task decomposition and reflective task adjustment, and Explorer, Verifier, Appraiser and Controller for per-subtask MCTS-based local optimization (goal-oriented selection, reflection-enhanced node expansion, dynamic evaluation and simulation, maximal value backpropagation)
extraction.benchmark: WebArena (812 human-annotated tasks across CMS, Map, Shopping, Reddit and GitLab) and MiniWoB++ (43 text-representable tasks); metric is success rate
extraction.baseline: the WebArena baseline agent, SteP (stacked expert-designed state-action policies), LM-Tree Search, RCI, AdaPlanner and a zero-shot agent, plus internal ablations removing Child Reflection, Sibling Reflection, Controller and Planner
extraction.key_results: 37.2% success rate on WebArena with GPT-4o versus 33.5% for SteP and 19.2% for LM-Tree Search, a 93% relative increase over the concurrent tree-search method; 29.1% with GPT-3.5 versus the 8.9% WebArena baseline; GitLab 39.4% versus SteP's 31.7% (a 7.7% improvement); 95.6% on MiniWoB++ against SteP's 96.0% while using 4 high-level demonstrations instead of SteP's 10 action-level ones. Moving from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4o inside the same architecture adds 11.8, 6.6 and 9.4 SR points on Shopping, Reddit and GitLab. Component ablations on 50 information-seeking and 50 website-interaction tasks drop success from 100%/100% to 74%/70% without Child Reflection, 72%/60% without Sibling Reflection, 86%/60% without Controller, and 48%/24% without Planner.
extraction.limitations: Authors state: effectiveness is limited by the capabilities of the underlying LLM, particularly in understanding and interacting with complex web environments through text-based actions; the absence of visual observation forces the LLM to infer context normally supplied by visual cues such as star counts; WebArena accessibility trees contain duplicated and non-interactive elements and some dropdown menus fail to expand, capping achievable performance; the ablation study is run on a curated subset of 100 tasks WebPilot had already solved, which the authors describe as isolating optimally functioning components.

evidence_notes.summary: WebPilot is a system paper whose comparisons illustrate the confound rather than control for it, which makes it useful as a RQ2 negative example alongside its ablation evidence. Its headline 93% relative gain over LM-Tree Search and its lead over SteP are whole-stack comparisons in which orchestration, prompting strategy and demonstration budget all differ simultaneously, since SteP uses 10 action-level demonstrations and expert-designed state-action policies while WebPilot uses 4 high-level demonstrations and MCTS-based exploration. Within its own architecture, however, the paper does isolate two factors cleanly. First, holding the architecture fixed and swapping GPT-3.5 for GPT-4o adds 11.8, 6.6 and 9.4 success-rate points across domains, a model effect of similar magnitude to the reported architectural advantage over SteP. Second, the component ablations show harness elements matter enormously in this setting, with removing the Planner dropping website-interaction success from 100% to 24% and removing Sibling Reflection dropping it to 60%. The ablations are run on a curated subset of tasks WebPilot already solved, so they establish component necessity rather than unbiased effect sizes.
